Retention means the act of keeping something, or the ability/state of holding onto something — without losing it, releasing it, or letting it leave.

The simplest way to think about it: whenever something could be lost, forgotten, discarded, or allowed to leave, but it is instead kept — that keeping is called retention.

It is a word about holding on.
The Two Main Flavors

Retention shows up in two slightly different ways:

  1. As an action or process — the deliberate act of keeping something.
    "The company focused on the retention of its best employees." (They worked actively to keep those employees.)
  2. As an ability or state — how well something naturally holds onto something else.
    "She has excellent retention." (Her mind naturally holds onto information well.)

Both flavors share the same root idea: something is being held, not lost.
Retention in Everyday Thinking

When you read a book and remember its ideas a week later, that's retention at work. When you study a concept and it "sticks," your brain has retained it.

When something fails to be retained, we say there is "poor retention" or that something "wasn't retained." For example, if you read a chapter and remember nothing the next day, you had low retention of that material.

This is why teachers and study techniques often talk about improving retention — meaning, making sure learned information stays in the mind rather than slipping away.
Retention in Memory and Learning

In the context of learning and memory, retention refers to how much of what you learned you actually remember over time.

  • Right after learning something, you might remember 100% of it.
  • After a week, without review, you might remember only 40%.
  • The percentage you still recall is your retention.

Good retention means information stays with you a long time. Poor retention means it fades quickly. Techniques like spaced repetition (revisiting material at increasing intervals) exist specifically to improve retention.

Retention here is not just about what you remember, but how durably and how accurately you hold onto it.
Retention in Business

This is one of the most common places you'll encounter the word today.

Customer retention means keeping existing customers — preventing them from leaving your business and going to a competitor. It is the opposite of churn (when customers leave). A business with high customer retention keeps most of its customers year over year. A business with low retention loses many of them.

Retention matters enormously in business because acquiring a new customer is usually far more expensive than keeping an existing one. So businesses invest heavily in retention strategies — loyalty programs, good customer service, discounts for long-term customers, and so on.

Employee retention (also called "talent retention") means keeping skilled workers in an organization. If employees keep quitting to join other companies, the organization has a retention problem. High retention means employees stay for a long time; low retention means high turnover.

You will also hear phrases like:

  • "Retention rate" — the percentage of customers/employees/users who stayed over a given period. A 90% annual customer retention rate means 90 out of 100 customers from last year are still customers today.
  • "Retention strategy" — a plan designed to prevent loss (of customers, employees, or users).
Retention in Medicine and Biology

In the human body, retention refers to the body holding onto a substance it would normally release or expel.

Water retention (also called fluid retention or edema) is when the body holds excess fluid in its tissues instead of flushing it out. This causes swelling, often in the legs, ankles, or hands. It can be caused by health conditions, medications, or diet (eating too much salt, for example, makes the body retain water).

Urinary retention is when the bladder cannot fully empty itself. The urine is being "retained" (held inside) even when it should be released.

In both cases, notice the pattern: something that should leave the body is instead being kept inside. That's retention.
Retention in Data and Technology

Data retention refers to how long a company, system, or platform keeps records before deleting them.

For example, a company might have a data retention policy that says: "We keep customer transaction records for 7 years, then delete them." During those 7 years, the data is being retained. After that, it is not.

Data retention policies exist because storing data has costs, and there are also legal and privacy reasons that govern how long certain data should be kept. Laws in many countries require businesses to retain certain records for minimum periods (e.g., tax records) and to not retain other data beyond a certain point (e.g., personal data under privacy laws like GDPR in Europe).
Retention in Finance

In finance, earnings retention (or "retained earnings") refers to the portion of a company's profits that it keeps to reinvest in the business, rather than paying out to shareholders as dividends.

If a company earns ₹100 crore in profit and pays out ₹30 crore as dividends, it retains ₹70 crore. That ₹70 crore is its retained earnings — money held back for growth, paying down debt, or future needs.
Retention in Law and Human Resources

A retainer (a related word) is a fee paid in advance to a lawyer or consultant to retain (keep) their services — to ensure they are available to you when needed.

In HR and legal contexts, document retention means keeping records, contracts, or files for the required period. Organizations are often legally obligated to retain certain documents (employment records, financial statements, legal correspondence) for specified years.
The Word's Full Range: A Summary

Across all these contexts, retention always means the same thing at its heart — keeping something that could otherwise be lost, released, or allowed to leave. What changes is what is being retained:

  • Information being retained in memory
  • Customers being retained by a business
  • Employees being retained by an employer
  • Fluid being retained in the body
  • Data being retained by a system
  • Earnings being retained by a company
  • Documents being retained for legal purposes
Nuances Worth Knowing

Retention implies something could leave. You don't use retention to describe keeping a rock in your hand; there's no natural force pulling it away. You use retention when there's a natural tendency toward loss — information fades from memory, customers switch brands, employees find new jobs, the body expels fluids, old data gets deleted. Retention is the force working against that natural loss.

High vs. low retention is a common way to quantify it. High retention = most of something is being kept. Low retention = much of it is being lost.

Retention is not hoarding or clinging. It has a neutral or positive tone in most contexts. Poor retention is a problem; good retention is a goal. The word doesn't carry a negative judgment by itself the way "hoarding" does — it simply describes the degree to which something is being held.

Retention vs. acquisition. In business especially, you'll see retention contrasted with acquisition. Acquisition is about getting new customers, employees, or users. Retention is about keeping the ones you already have. Both are needed; neglecting either creates problems.
